## Brand Strategy
- "One Ogilvy" -- streamlined name as part of simplifying the network
- Eliminated disciplines, created new collaborative approach, streamlined offering, expanded capabilities
- Brand architecture: "Ogilvy is a singular, creative network creating design, experiences and communications that make brands matter"
- Only one branded sub-entity: Ogilvy Consulting (enterprise offering)
- Full legal name remains "The Ogilvy Group"
- Document dated September 9, 2019

## Logo
- Custom logotype -- evolution of predecessor (bears structural resemblance to Baskerville but entirely new typeface design)
- Notable ligatures: g+i connect, i+l connect at serif, v+y connect at serif -- creating a logogram
- Default color: Ogilvy Red
- Logo colors restricted to: black, white, or Ogilvy Red only
- Width-to-height ratio: 330:129 -- specific ratio check method provided (set width to 330, height must be 129.04)
- Ligatures described as adding "distinction and sophistication" -- they also play a role in the broader brand typography system

## Outliers
- Dedicated "David Ogilvy" section (5 pages) -- rare for a brand guide to have a section about the founder as a brand element
- The ligature system (logo letterforms connecting) extending into general typography is a sophisticated design decision
- An advertising agency's own brand guidelines -- meta-level interest as practitioners codifying their own identity
- "One Ogilvy" rebrand eliminated all sub-brands (OgilvyOne, Ogilvy & Mather, etc.) -- significant simplification
- Precise ratio-checking methodology for logo distortion is unusually technical and practical

## Quality Score
- **Score: 4/5** -- Comprehensive 74-page guide from a leading advertising agency covering logo, color, typography, digital, publications, stationery, and branded collateral. Strong brand strategy articulation with the "One Ogilvy" narrative. The ligature-based identity system and David Ogilvy heritage section show sophisticated brand thinking. Missing dedicated photography and graphics sections, and tone of voice is implicit rather than explicitly codified.
